summary: This short program creates three House objects — one for each famous fictional address — and tries to print each one with System.out.println. The output is not what you would hope for, which is exactly the lesson.

lines.code: House privetDrive = new House("4 Privet Drive", 3, 2.5);
lines.text: Each call to new builds a brand-new House object in memory and hands back a reference to it, which we store in a variable. The three values in parentheses are passed to the constructor in the order it declares them: address, bedrooms, then bathrooms.

Printing an object does not print its fields. Java quietly calls the object's toString method, and since House has not supplied one, you get the inherited default: the class name plus an @ and a hexadecimal hash code, such as House@1b6d3586.

lines.code: House holmesHouse = new House("221B Baker Street", 1, 1.0);
lines.text: Notice that 1.0 is written with a decimal point because the bathrooms field is a double; passing a whole-number literal like 1 would work here through automatic widening, but writing 1.0 makes the type you mean obvious.

lines.code: House friendsHouse = new House("90 Bedford Street", 2, 1.0);
lines.text: Three separate objects now exist from the same class, each with its own copy of the fields. The class is the blueprint; these are three independent houses built from it.
